title: The Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen Argument in Quantum Theory

summaries.example: Imagine two special boxes that are prepared together and then carried far apart. If opening one box tells you exactly what is in it, you can use that information to predict what is in the other box. EPR asked whether the second box already had that feature before anyone looked, or whether looking at the first box somehow changed what could be said about the second.
summaries.summary: The Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen argument, usually called EPR, is a famous challenge about what quantum theory means. Quantum theory uses a mathematical object called a wave function to predict the results of measurements. EPR imagined two quantum systems that had interacted and then moved far apart. Their positions and motions could be linked so closely that measuring one system would let someone predict a matching fact about the other. EPR argued that the distant system must already have definite facts about it, because the measurement did not directly disturb it. But the wave function did not contain both kinds of definite facts together. So, they said, quantum theory was not complete. Niels Bohr answered that a measurement changes the conditions under which we can describe and predict the other system, even without a simple physical push or bump. The disagreement is about reality, measurement, and whether quantum theory gives a full picture of nature. The argument later influenced studies of entanglement, spin, and Bell inequalities.
key_ideas: Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen asked whether quantum theory tells us everything important about quantum systems.
Their argument used two linked systems that could be very far apart.
They thought a faraway measurement should not directly change the other system.
They concluded that the wave function might not give a complete description.
Bohr disagreed about what it means for a quantity to be real or to be disturbed by a measurement.
Later versions used spin and helped inspire Bell’s work on quantum correlations.
summaries.why_it_matters: EPR matters because it asks a basic question about science: does a theory describe the world itself, or only what we can observe? It also helped lead to important work on quantum entanglement and information. The argument shows that a small, strange-looking science puzzle can raise large questions about knowledge and reality.

important_terms.definition: A theory is complete if it includes every important fact needed to describe what is happening.
A link between two separated quantum systems, so that learning something about one helps predict something about the other.
The idea that an action here cannot directly change what is real in a faraway system.
A carefully imagined situation used to explore an idea, even when it is difficult to perform in a laboratory.

questions_to_think_about: If you can predict something with certainty, does that prove it was already true?
Can two things be connected even when they are far apart?
What should a scientific theory explain: only observations, or also what exists when nobody is looking?
Why might different scientists use the same experiment to support different ideas?

summaries.example: Consider two systems prepared in a joint quantum state and then separated into distant laboratories. If measuring system A’s position lets us predict system B’s position with certainty, and measuring A’s momentum instead lets us predict B’s momentum with certainty, the EPR reasoning treats both quantities as definite for B. This depends on locality: a measurement at A does not directly alter the reality of B. Yet quantum mechanics does not assign a single state vector that gives both position and momentum definite values. EPR therefore argues that the state-vector description is incomplete.
summaries.summary:
The Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen argument examines whether quantum mechanics provides a complete description of physical reality. The issue arose partly from a disagreement between Einstein’s realist concerns and Bohr’s interpretation of measurement and complementarity. In the original EPR paper, two systems are prepared in an entangled state and then separated. Their positions and momenta remain strictly correlated. EPR propose that if a quantity can be predicted with certainty without disturbing a system, that quantity has a corresponding element of physical reality. They also rely on separability, according to which each distant system has its own physical state, and locality, according to which a measurement on one system does not directly change the reality of the other. These assumptions allow them to infer simultaneous definite position and momentum for a system, although no quantum state represents both as definite. They conclude that the quantum state-vector description is incomplete.

The entry emphasizes that this is not the only EPR argument. Einstein’s own later presentations generally avoid the original criterion of reality and do not depend on simultaneous values for incompatible quantities. Instead, they frame a dilemma: locality and separability cannot both be maintained with a complete description of individual systems by quantum state functions. Bohr’s reply denies that the EPR criterion can be used so straightforwardly. A distant measurement may not mechanically disturb the second system, he argues, but it changes the conditions under which predictions about that system are defined. The clarity and consistency of this response remain difficult philosophical issues.

key_ideas: The original EPR paper connects completeness with whether incompatible quantities, especially position and momentum, can possess simultaneous definite values.
Its central reasoning combines a certainty-based reality criterion, separability, and locality.

The EPR paper’s argument is not identical to Einstein’s later versions. Einstein often focused more simply on a conflict between locality-separability and a complete description of individual systems.
Bohr accepted that there was no ordinary mechanical disturbance of the distant system, but argued that the measurement changes the conditions for making predictions about it.

Bohm’s spin version made the EPR situation more suitable for experimental analysis. Bell later showed that quantum correlations conflict with inequalities derived from assumptions including a form of locality, though the exact assumptions matter.

The debate does not automatically establish one simple conclusion such as “quantum theory is definitely nonlocal” or “the wave function is definitely complete.” Different interpretations may question different assumptions.
summaries.why_it_matters: EPR matters because it exposes the interpretive assumptions hidden inside a mathematical theory. It distinguishes predicting an outcome from describing an underlying property, and it forces careful attention to locality, separability, and measurement. Its descendants, including the Bohm version and Bell’s theorem, helped connect philosophical questions about quantum reality with experimentally testable correlations and with quantum information theory.

important_terms.definition: The claim that every physically relevant truth about a system is represented in its quantum state or state vector.
A quantum description, often called a wave function or state vector, used to calculate probabilities for measurement outcomes.
The claim that spatially separated systems possess their own physical states or identities.
The claim that a measurement on one separated system does not directly change the reality pertaining to the other.
EPR’s sufficient condition: if a quantity can be predicted with certainty without disturbing a system, it corresponds to an element of physical reality.
A quantity is definite when the system’s underlying real state assigns it a particular value.
A situation in which two quantum systems have correlations that cannot be represented as merely independent descriptions of each system.
Inequalities derived under certain assumptions about correlations; some quantum predictions and experiments violate them.

questions_to_think_about: Does certainty of prediction show that a property existed before measurement, or could it show only something about the measurement context?

summaries.example: Suppose two students receive two sealed, specially prepared cards. The cards are sent to different towns. If one student asks a question of the first card and can then predict the answer the second card would give, there are two possibilities: the second card already carried the relevant answer, or the first question somehow changed what could be true about the distant card. EPR used a much more precise quantum version of this puzzle, involving position and momentum rather than ordinary cards.
summaries.summary:
The Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen argument asks whether quantum mechanics gives a complete account of physical reality. At the time, one influential approach associated with Niels Bohr emphasized that measurement involves an interaction with an apparatus and that some pairs of quantities, such as position and momentum, cannot both be precisely determined in one measurement context. Einstein worried that this made the theory describe only what happens when observers measure, rather than what systems are like independently of observation.

EPR considered two quantum systems that had interacted and then moved far apart. Their joint quantum state links their positions and also their momenta. Measuring one system’s position allows the position of the other to be predicted with certainty; measuring one system’s momentum similarly allows the other momentum to be predicted. EPR proposed that a quantity predictable with certainty, without disturbing the system, corresponds to a real, definite feature. They also assumed separability and locality: distant systems have their own physical states, and a measurement on one does not directly change the reality of the other. From these assumptions, they argued that the distant system has definite values for both position and momentum. Yet quantum mechanics has no state that represents both as definite together. The conclusion is that the quantum description is incomplete.

The source also separates this original argument from Einstein’s later versions. Einstein often focused on a broader conflict between locality and a complete description of individual systems, without relying on simultaneous position and momentum values. key_ideas: EPR was a 1935 argument by Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen about whether quantum mechanics is complete.
The argument begins with two systems whose positions and momenta are strictly correlated, even after the systems separate.
EPR says that certainty without disturbance supports the claim that a quantity has a definite value.
If locality and separability are accepted, the distant system seems to have definite position and definite momentum at once.
Quantum mechanics does not provide a wave function that assigns both values together, so EPR argues that its description leaves something out.
Bohr challenges the way EPR understands disturbance and reality; later work by Bohm and Bell develops the issue in new forms.
summaries.why_it_matters: The EPR debate matters because it teaches that scientific disagreements can concern interpretation, not just calculation. Two thinkers may agree on experimental predictions while disagreeing about what the mathematics says exists. The argument also became a starting point for discussions of entanglement, spin experiments, Bell inequalities, and the uses of quantum correlations in quantum information.

important_terms.definition: The idea that a scientific description contains all the physically important facts about the system it describes.
A strong connection between quantum systems that can make results on one system highly predictable from results on another.
The view that separated objects have their own physical condition, even when their properties are correlated.
The view that measuring one distant system does not directly alter the physical reality of another separated system.
A rule proposed by EPR: certain prediction with no disturbance is evidence that the predicted quantity is a real feature of the system.
A quantum description, represented mathematically by a wave function or state vector, that gives probabilities for measurement results.
Two quantities that quantum theory does not allow to be represented as having precise values together in one ordinary quantum state.

questions_to_think_about: Is predicting a result with certainty enough to show that the result was already a fact?
Why does EPR distinguish a physical disturbance from a change in the conditions for prediction?
Could a theory be statistically successful while still failing to describe everything that is real?
What assumptions would have to be changed to avoid the EPR conclusion?
Why might a philosophical argument about measurement lead to experiments?
